Selected Projects / DARI
Case study · Product & prototype
DARI
Your words, ready for care.

A pre-visit companion that helps aging immigrant patients explain health concerns in their own cultural language — and turns them into a clear summary a doctor can use.

🏆Best
Pitch
ContextSKKU × University of Toronto international entrepreneurship bootcamp · 4 weeks, Summer 2026
Team4 people, Korea × Canada
My roleProduct & technical prototype — technology, engineering and product execution
OutputWorking app prototype + investor-style pitch
ResultBest Pitch & Cultural Awareness awards

How we got from a problem to an award

  1. 01Define the problem
  2. 02Listen to experts
  3. 03Position the product
  4. 04Design the journey
  5. 05Build the prototype
  6. 06Design for risk
  7. 07Make the business case
  8. 🏆Pitch & win
01 Define the problem

The gap isn’t just language.

Older immigrant parents describe symptoms with folk-health words. Their adult children translate under stress. Doctors receive fragments.

30%limited English15 minper visit
Before building anything, I asked the uncomfortable question: “Doesn’t ChatGPT already do this?” The answer became our edge — translating cultural meaning, not just words.
02 Listen to experts

3 interviews → 3 design rules.

  • 1Hospital nurse: family interpreting adds bias → support caregivers, don’t make them the interpreter
  • 2Community nurse: seniors talk in stories → listen first, structure later
  • 3TCM practitioner: clinicians read structured notes → output must fit SOAP
Research decided the features — not the other way round.
03 Position the product

Not a doctor. Not a translator. A pre-visit assistant.

  • 1Listen in their own language, dialect and folk terms
  • 2Clarify onset, severity and context — without diagnosing
  • 3Summarize into a bilingual note the patient confirms
🎯 Start narrow: Cantonese-speaking seniors in Toronto
Saying clearly what Dari is not kept both the scope and the team honest.
04 Design the journey

One guided journey, four steps.

  • 1Set up — patient, caregiver or both
  • 2Languages & region — so Dari uses familiar terms
  • 3Tell the story — by voice or text
  • 4Confirm & share — the patient approves the summary
Asking for region, not just language, lets Dari pick the right regional words — without making assumptions about the person.
05 Build the prototype

A working app, not just mockups.

  • ⚙RAG on a 5-layer glossary: TCM, Western clinical, medication, regional terms, clarification rules
  • 🔒Runs on a private server
  • ⇄Bilingual conversation and transcript
  • 📄Clinician summary + SOAP view, shared by email or PDF
I built the API, the RAG pipeline, the data cleaning and the prototype itself.
06 Design for risk

We pitched where it could fail.

In healthcare, an AI that guesses is dangerous. So every term gets a confidence label — and the product behaves differently for each.

DIRECT
Clear term → translate and show the source
INTERPRETED
Likely meaning → patient must confirm
UNCERTAIN
Risky meaning → ask, never guess
✕ Never diagnose✕ Never invent details✓ Patient confirms before sharing
Most teams showed features. We also showed our risks — AI hallucination — and exactly how the product handles them.
07 Make the business case

A business that grows with trust.

  • 1Free — build trust with families first
  • 2Dari Plus — subscription concept, only after validation
  • 3Institutions — clinics and care agencies, after proof of use
Target: ≥50% 7-day activationTarget: ≥3/5 post-chat rating
Every number was framed as a test to run, not a result we already had.
🏆

Best Pitch
+ Cultural Awareness

Judged by Canadian and Korean professors, organizers and startup professionals.

What I took away

Define before you build.Questioning the premise early gave us a sharper problem — and a real reason to exist.
Design the failure modes.Showing how the product handles risk built more trust than another feature would have.
Start narrow, earn trust.One community, one high-stakes workflow, clear tests — then expand.

Selected Projects / Master’s thesis
Master’s thesis · Sungkyunkwan University · 2026
Easy to read.
Easy to trust?

Does adding pictures and voice to an AI medical translation help people understand it — or mainly make them trust it more?

Full title: Exploring the Effectiveness of Multimodal AI Medical Translation Interfaces on Comprehension, Cognitive Load, Trust, and Behavioral Intention

DegreeM.S. Interaction Science (Human-AI Interaction), SKKU
MethodOnline controlled experiment · 3 randomly assigned groups
BuiltA custom AI translation app used as the test environment
AnalysisSerial mediation (PROCESS Model 6, 5,000 bootstrap samples) + robustness checks
Key resultThe benefit of multimodal design ran through trust, not comprehension

From a question to a design insight

  1. 01Ask the question
  2. 02Build the model
  3. 03Design the experiment
  4. 04Control the test app
  5. 05Measure & analyze
  6. 06Findings
  7. 💡What it means
01 Ask the question

Same words. Different format. Different reaction?

Health apps now show AI-generated guidance as text, text with images, or text with images and voice. Medical instructions are high-stakes — so how the information is presented may matter as much as what it says.

This study does not test translation accuracy or clinical safety. It keeps the content identical and changes only the presentation.
Text“Take the pen out of the fridge…”
+ Image🧊 → ⏱ 15 min
+ Audio🔊 “Let’s go through it step by step…”
Which one helps you understand?
Which one makes you trust it?
02 Build the model

Two possible routes to “I’d use this”.

  • AComprehension route: less mental effort → better understanding → more willing to use it
  • BTrust route: less mental effort feels easy → easy feels trustworthy → more willing to use it
Earlier research studied these two routes separately. Testing both in one model shows which one actually does the work.
03 Design the experiment

3 groups. One change at a time.

  • 1Text only — the baseline
  • 2Text + image — adds a visual channel
  • 3Text + image + audio — adds a guiding voice
🎲 Random assignment📐 Power analysis before recruiting
The voice does not read the screen word-for-word. It guides, like a person walking you through it — reading the same text twice would add effort, not reduce it.
04 Control the test app

I built the app so only the format could change.

Participants used a custom AI translation app to read a foreign prescription label for an injectable medicine. Every possible source of noise was locked down.

No typingInput limited to photo upload — no typos, no partial input
One preloaded photoUpload opened a fixed album with only the target label
Identical translationsOutputs were pre-generated and the same in every group
Audio plays itselfNarration started automatically, so exposure didn’t depend on choice
Quality checksAttention checks + a voice check to confirm people really listened
05 Measure & analyze

Four things measured, one chain tested.

Established scales, adapted to this context, plus an objective test.

Serial mediation tests whether the effect travels through the steps in order — not just whether the start and end are related. The result was then re-checked controlling for age, gender, education and country.
Mental effortExtraneous cognitive load · 5 itemsα = .947
TrustTrust in the AI system · 6 itemsα = .927
Comprehension10-question multiple-choice testobjective
Intention to useUTAUT-based · 3 itemsα = .894
06 Findings

Easier to read → more trusted → more likely to be used.

① Adding image + audio lowered mental effort
Text only10.44
+ Image9.19
+ Image + Audio7.70

Mean extraneous load (lower = easier). Text + image + audio was significantly lower than text only (p = .007); text + image alone was not.

≈26% lower
② That ease worked through trust — not understanding

Serial indirect effect through mental effort and trust: 0.437, 95% CI [0.130, 0.847]. Still significant after controlling for demographics.

Hypothesis scoreboard
H1More modalities → less effort✓
H2Less effort → better understanding✗
H3Understanding → intention✗
H4Comprehension route✗
H5Less effort → more trust✓
H6Trust → intention✓
H7Trust route✓
The comprehension route wasn’t supported here. The instructions were short and simple, and test scores varied little — so the format had little room to change understanding. Longer, more complex content may behave differently.

What it means for design

Ease builds trust.A clearer, multimodal format can make people more willing to rely on a health AI tool.
But ease isn’t accuracy.Feeling easy can raise trust on its own — so pair it with transparency and confidence cues, and verify accuracy separately.
Measure trust on its own.When evaluating patient-facing AI, treat trust as its own outcome — alongside, not instead of, understanding.
Limits I’m upfront about Mostly U.S. English speakersOne short medication instructionMeasured once, not over timeComprehension test with low variance
Skills used Research question & theory buildingExperimental designPower analysisBuilding a test appSurvey measurementMediation analysisAcademic writing
Selected Projects / AI Musician
Co-authored research · AAA Lab, Sungkyunkwan University
Would you play
a song by AI?

AI can now write songs in seconds. We asked what actually makes people willing to listen to, pay for and recommend them — how the AI behaves, or what everyone else thinks.

Paper: When AI Is Perceived as a Musician: The Role of Social Perception in AI Music Consumption (manuscript)

TeamLab research with fellow researchers at AAA Lab, SKKU
MethodOnline 2 × 2 × 2 experiment · 8 randomly assigned conditions
BuiltA chatbot “AI musician” that turns a love letter into a song
AnalysisANOVA, regression, manipulation checks, reliability & validity tests
Key resultGetting the request right mattered — social pressure didn’t

From a question to a design insight

  1. 01Ask the question
  2. 02Build the model
  3. 03Design 8 conditions
  4. 04Build the AI musician
  5. 05Check the setup
  6. 06Findings
  7. 💡What it means
01 Ask the question

Tool, or musician?

AI music services are growing fast. But making songs is easy — getting people to choose them is the hard part. We tested three things that might make the difference.

For any AI creative service, adoption depends less on what the model can do and more on how people perceive it.
TalkDoes it chat with you while creating?
FitDoes it give you what you asked for?
CrowdDoes everyone else already use it?
Which one makes people
listen, buy and share?
02 Build the model

Inside the experience vs. outside pressure.

  • AInside: people treat computers like social actors (CASA). So chatting and adapting might make the AI feel like a real musician → better attitude → more listening.
  • BOutside: the bandwagon effect — if “everyone uses it”, maybe you will too.
Testing both in one study shows whether choices are driven by the product experience or by the crowd.
03 Design 8 conditions

3 switches × 2 settings = 8 versions.

Each participant was randomly assigned one combination, so every factor could be tested on its own and together.

🎲 Random assignment📐 Power analysis before recruiting
Interactivity6-turn conversation1 single prompt
AdaptabilitySong matches chosen genreDifferent genre
Public opinion“Most people use AI music”“Few people do”
Simplified illustration of the two article versions
04 Build the AI musician

Write a love letter. Get a song.

  • 1Participants wrote a short love letter to a chatbot “AI musician” (built in Landbot)
  • 2They picked a genre: country, rock or jazz — easy to recognise without music training
  • 3They heard “their” song — actually pre-made, with the same lyrics for everyone
  • 4They were told the truth afterwards in a full debrief
Both chat versions asked for about the same amount of writing and took about the same time — so “more turns” didn’t simply mean “more effort”.
AI Musician
Hi! I’ll turn your love letter into a song 🎵
Who is this letter for?
My partner
How did you first meet?
At a café in the rain ☔
Which genre would you like?
CountryRockJazz
Illustration of the 6-turn version
05 Check the setup

Did people notice the differences?

Before reading any results, we checked that the manipulations worked and that the measures were solid.

If participants hadn’t noticed the genre mismatch or the article, a “no effect” would mean nothing.
Adaptability noticedWrong-genre group felt the AI adapted far lesslarge effect · d = 1.14
Public opinion noticedArticle version clearly changed what people believedlarge effect · d = 1.04
Attention checksDid the song have lyrics? Which genre was it?quality control
Solid measuresReliability, factor loadings, KMO & Bartlett’s testα = .70 – .90
06 Findings

Get it right > talk more > follow the crowd.

① What moved people
✓AdaptabilityA song in the genre people asked for raised consumption intentionp = .036
✗Interactivity6 chat turns vs. 1 prompt made no differencep = .254
✗Public opinion“Everyone uses it” didn’t change choicesp = .763
53%

Attitude toward the AI musician explained about half of the differences in consumption intention (β = .73).

② The path that worked

Interactivity and adaptability did not change attitude. Adaptability worked directly — more like a sign of competence than of “social” warmth.

Hypothesis scoreboard
H1Interactivity → consumption✗
H2Adaptability → consumption✓
H3Interactivity → attitude✗
H4Adaptability → attitude✗
H5Attitude → consumption✓
H6Public opinion → consumption✗
More conversation and social proof sound like obvious wins — here they weren’t. People seemed to judge AI music on their own experience of it, not on what others do.

What it means for AI products

Get the request right.Accurately delivering what users asked for drove use more than extra conversation did.
Don’t lean on hype.“Everyone’s using it” messaging didn’t move people — their own experience did.
Shape how the AI is seen.People who saw the AI as a credible creative agent were far more willing to listen and pay.
Limits we’re upfront about Music only — images or text may differIntention, not actual purchasesPublic opinion shown as a scenario
Skills used Factorial experimental designChatbot prototyping (Landbot)Stimulus designSurvey measurementANOVA & regressionCollaborative academic writing

Service design · Seoul AI Smart City idea competition · 2026
YONGSAN
PAUSE ‖
A city where you’re allowed to stop.

An AI service that connects a future district’s empty spaces with people who need a rest — free, without a reason, and without an app.

BriefAI smart city ideas for Seoul’s Yongsan International Business District (2040)
CategoryService
My roleConcept, service design, AI logic, user journey and the final presentation board
Output16:9 competition board + written proposal, submitted Nov 2026

From a city problem to a service

  1. 01Frame the problem
  2. 02Find the insight
  3. 03Design the service
  4. 04Design the AI
  5. 05Design for trust
  6. 06Map the journey
  7. ‖Roll it out
01 Frame the problem

A faster city — where resting costs money.

In 2040, Yongsan becomes a dense vertical hub of rail, offices and conventions. Moving gets faster. But the only places to sit down are mostly cafés.

  • 1Long-distance traveller — an hour before the meeting, nowhere to go but a café
  • 2Older pedestrian — a huge multi-level district, no place to pause
  • 3Global worker — after an overnight call, needs a quick nap
02 Find the insight

The space already exists. The connection doesn’t.

Building new rest spaces in a dense city is expensive. Yet rooftop gardens, terraces, office lobbies and convention halls sit empty for much of the day.

100%+green-space target vs. lot area19.0%parks & green space in the district
Don’t build — borrow. Turn a construction problem into a matching problem, which is exactly what AI is good at.
03 Design the service

Four kinds of pause — short to long.

The darker the colour, the longer the rest. One system, four needs.

☀️❄️😷 Climate mode: during heatwaves, cold snaps or fine-dust alerts, more indoor spaces open automatically — the network becomes a climate shelter.
04 Design the AI

AI watches empty spaces, not people.

It only uses data that can’t identify anyone: train delays, event schedules, weather and air quality, and anonymous occupancy.

A big conference ends in 30 minutes → the AI opens nearby terraces and lounges before the crowd arrives.
PAUSE
AI
1Register empty spaceBuildings list idle times
2Predict demandAnonymous data only
3Decide what opensWhere & when, automatically
4Guide with lightFloor & wall lights — no app
5Learn & improveUsage, cleaning, repairs
05 Design for trust

A smart city that doesn’t watch you.

Rest is private. If people feel tracked, they won’t use it — so privacy is a design rule, not an afterthought.

✕ No Camera✕ No Account✕ No Score
No sign-up and light-based guidance also mean older people, wheelchair users and foreign visitors can use it equally — no smartphone needed.
NO CAMERA
No face recognition, no cameras inside rest spaces
NO ACCOUNT
No app install or sign-up — just walk in
NO SCORE
Nobody is rated or recorded; basic use is free
06 Map the journey

A business traveller’s day — three pauses.

11:40Arrives at Yongsan Station by KTX
11:45PAUSE 05 · 8 min rest, phone charged
11:55Walks 6 min to the convention centre
12:10PAUSE 40 · 42 min deep rest before the meeting
13:00Joins the meeting, refreshed
15:30PAUSE OPEN · unwinds on a terrace

No money spent. No sign-up.

Roll it out step by step

1 · PilotTest at a transit hub, a convention venue and an outdoor green link.
2 · GrowAdd offices and shops, with incentives for buildings that share space.
3 · ConnectLink the whole district into one rest network, with climate mode always on.
How success would be measuredSpace utilisationAverage wait timeParticipating buildingsUser satisfaction

Selected Projects / When the AI Advisor Is Wrong
Solo research paper · 2026
What if the
AI is wrong?

Millions of people now ask AI chatbots about their health. I built a virtual town of 5,000 people to test when an imperfect — and sometimes flattering — AI stops health rumors, and when it spreads them.

Paper: When the AI Advisor Is Wrong: Trust Dynamics, Sycophancy, and Health-Literacy Asymmetries in Misinformation Dynamics

RoleSole author — question, model, experiments, analysis and writing
StatusUnder peer review at the Journal of Computational Social Science (Springer)
MethodComputer simulation (agent-based model) built in NetLogo
Scale1,000,000+ simulated runs across 1,223 scenarios
OpenCode and data publicly archived on Zenodo

From a question to a design insight

  1. 01Ask the question
  2. 02Build a virtual town
  3. 03Set the rules first
  4. 04Run 1M+ simulations
  5. 05Findings
  6. 06Stress-test
  7. 💡What it means
01 Ask the question

AI aces medical exams. Real users don’t get the same AI.

Tested alone, AI models found the right condition in about 95% of medical scenarios. When ordinary people used the same models, they got it right in under 35% of cases. And AI assistants tend to agree with whatever you already believe — called sycophancy.

17%of US adults ask AI chatbots about health monthly95% → 35%benchmark vs. real use
Rumors spread through friends and family. You can’t safely release a bad AI into a real community to watch what happens — but you can in a model.
AccuracyHow good must the AI be to help, not harm?
FlatteryWhat if it agrees with people’s wrong beliefs?
FairnessAre people with lower health literacy left behind?
And does it change the minds of people
who never use it?
02 Build a virtual town

5,000 people. One false health claim. Two years.

Each virtual person has a belief in the claim, a level of health literacy and a level of trust in the AI. They live in a realistic social network — a few people have many friends, most have a few.

  • ⚙I can turn four dials: AI accuracy, how much it flatters, how many people use it, and the town’s health literacy
  • ⚖Trust is lopsided, like in real life: a noticed mistake costs 3× more trust than a good answer earns
What happens every simulated day
1
The rumor spreadsPeople who believe it pass it on to friends
2
Friends talk it overSimilar opinions pull closer together
3
Some ask the AIThe answer nudges what they believe
4
They judge the answerSpot a mistake → trust drops; higher literacy spots more
03 Set the rules first

Decide what “success” means before seeing results.

The questions, predictions and decision rules were written down before the main experiments ran — so results couldn’t be cherry-picked afterwards.

Every part of the model was tested on its own first. The rumor engine was checked against a well-known real-world finding: false news spreads further and deeper than true news.
HELPS
The AI cuts the share of misinformed people by at least 2 points — and the least literate aren’t worse off
UNCLEAR
The effect is too small or too uncertain to call
HARMS
The AI raises the share of misinformed people by more than 2 points
04 Run 1M+ simulations

Every AI town gets a twin town without AI.

Each run was paired with an identical town — same people, same friendships, same rumor — but no AI. The difference between the twins is the AI’s true effect.

Random chance can look like an effect. Twin towns plus hundreds of repeats per setting make the comparison fair and precise.
1,000,000+simulated town-runsscale
1,223combinations of the four dialscoverage
330 – 2,000repeats per setting, until results were preciseprecision
2 yearsof daily life simulated in each runtime
05 Findings

A barely-better-than-chance AI can help — unless it flatters.

① The “safe zone” map

Blue = the AI reduces misinformation. Red = it makes it worse. Without flattery, an AI only 51–54% accurate already helped — because it pushes people away from the rumor more often than towards it. More users made both the good and the bad effects bigger.

② Flattery raises the bar

The more the AI agrees with wrong beliefs, the more accurate it must be to help: up to 61–66% at the strongest flattery. Simple math said a flattering AI would trap believers forever (dashed line) — but in a real social network the trap leaks: people stumble out of it, and friends pull them back.

③ Unequal use, nearly equal outcomes

People with low health literacy missed about twice as many AI mistakes (≈50% vs. ≈24%). Yet the AI’s effect on who ended up misinformed was almost the same for everyone — within 2 points in 1,204 of 1,223 scenarios. Where it did differ, low-literacy users were worse off, by up to 2.2 points.

④ The ripple effect
0.28

Through everyday conversations, the AI shifted the beliefs of people who never used it — by up to 0.28 on a 0–1 scale, for better or for worse depending on how good the AI was.

Turn off conversations in the model, and the ripple disappears.

Predictions scoreboard
8supported
3not supported
1reported descriptively
I predicted that more health-literate people would abandon even good AI. They didn’t: people mostly abandoned bad AIs, and accurate ones were almost never dropped. That’s a better outcome than expected — and worth reporting as it is.
06 Stress-test

Would the answer survive different assumptions?

  • 9The model was re-run under 9 alternative assumptions — e.g. people weighting advice more, or no conversations at all
  • ✓“Flattery raises the bar” held in every version where it could be measured
  • !The exact accuracy needed shifted with assumptions — so it’s reported as conditional, not as one magic number
A global sensitivity analysis showed AI accuracy and flattery matter more than any assumption about human behavior — and how believable the rumor is matters most of all.

What it means for AI health products

Test the accuracy users get.Benchmark scores aren’t the accuracy real people experience — evaluate the AI in use.
Don’t just agree.An AI that flatters users needs to be much more accurate to do any good. Reducing sycophancy is a safety feature.
Look beyond your users.An AI’s answers ripple through families and friends — its impact reaches people who never open the app.
Limits I’m upfront about A simulation, not real peopleOne false claim at a timeLiteracy only affects trust in this modelExact numbers depend on assumptions

A Little About Me

Hi, I'm Wei-Ting Chang, originally from Taiwan and currently based in Seoul, South Korea.

I completed my undergraduate studies in Politics and Media at the University of Auckland in New Zealand, including an exchange period at Yonsei University in South Korea. I later pursued a master's degree in Interaction Science at Sungkyunkwan University, focusing on Human–AI Interaction, user behavior, and technology-mediated experiences.

My academic background may seem quite diverse at first, but for me, these fields are closely connected. They have gradually shaped the way I understand people, technology, products, and markets.

‖

How It All Started

My interest in user experience began during my undergraduate studies in media, long before I formally studied human–computer interaction.

Through my academic projects and practical experiences, I had opportunities to work with websites, digital content, and online communication. One particularly meaningful experience was contributing to the website redesign planning of an NGO in Spain.

While working on these projects, I began to notice that a website could contain valuable information and still fail to communicate effectively. Some websites were visually appealing but difficult to navigate. Others made important information unnecessarily difficult to find or did not adequately consider the accessibility needs of different users.

I became increasingly interested in questions that went beyond visual appearance: Who is this service actually designed for? Can people easily find what they need? Why are certain functions designed this way? What prevents users from completing a seemingly simple task?

That was when I began to understand UX as a discipline that extends far beyond UI and visual design. It involves understanding human behavior, identifying problems, structuring information, and making products and services more effective and accessible.

Over time, this interest also became part of my everyday life.

When using a banking app, shopping online, booking a flight, or staying at a hotel, I often find myself paying attention to how the entire experience is structured. At hotels, for example, I notice not only the physical facilities but also the check-in process, service efficiency, staff communication, and the consistency of the overall experience.

I also genuinely enjoy writing detailed reviews—not simply to express whether I liked something, but to explain what worked well, what did not, and how the experience could potentially be improved.

These observations gradually encouraged me to pursue a more systematic understanding of user experience, human behavior, and technology.

‖

Why Korea?

My decision to move from New Zealand to South Korea was influenced by both my previous exchange experience at Yonsei University and my growing interest in digital products and services.

Having lived in different countries and experienced a variety of digital platforms, I became particularly interested in the quality of South Korea's digital services.

Banking applications are one example. Among the banking services I have personally used across different countries, Korean banking apps stand out for their visual consistency, intuitive interactions, convenience, and integration of everyday financial services.

What interests me is not simply how these applications look, but how effectively their functions are organized and how they respond to users' everyday needs.

Beyond digital products, I am also interested in South Korea as a consumer market. The country offers an interesting environment for observing how consumers respond to emerging technologies, new services, international brands, and changing trends.

For example, Chipotle's decision to open its first Asian restaurant in Seoul illustrates why South Korea is an interesting market to observe when studying international expansion, consumer behavior, and the adoption of new products and services.

These experiences motivated me to continue my education at Sungkyunkwan University, where I could explore the relationships between people, technology, and interactive systems in greater depth.

‖

Beyond AI: My Broader Interests

Although my master's research focused on Human–AI Interaction, my interests are not limited to artificial intelligence or software interfaces.

I am interested in understanding how products and services work as a whole—from the initial identification of user needs and market opportunities to functionality, accessibility, business strategy, implementation, and evaluation.

This includes digital platforms, mobile applications, AI-powered services, consumer technology, and international product localization.

My interests have also expanded beyond screen-based experiences to emerging technologies such as robotics, autonomous vehicles, drones, smart mobility, and technology-enabled physical services.

What interests me most is not necessarily the technology itself, but how it can be applied in ways that are useful, accessible, commercially viable, and meaningful to the people who use it.

I enjoy examining products from multiple perspectives: the user, the business, the market, and the technology behind them.

This is also why my portfolio brings together academic research, product and service planning, business analysis, international projects, and independent explorations rather than focusing on a single professional discipline.

‖

Languages & Global Experience

Growing up in Taiwan, studying in New Zealand, and continuing my education in South Korea have given me opportunities to experience different cultures, consumer environments, educational systems, and approaches to communication.

I work across Mandarin Chinese, English, and Korean. These language skills allow me to access information from different markets, understand regional perspectives, and communicate across cultural boundaries.

My international experiences have also encouraged me to consider how the same product or service may be perceived differently across markets, and how businesses can adapt their strategies to meet different cultural and consumer needs.

Moving forward, I hope to apply this interdisciplinary and international background to projects involving product and service planning, AI applications, global business development, and data-driven decision-making.
